readme.de:
# Eigene Karte

Ein Tile, das du selbst zusammenstellst: Werte, Ringe, Balken, Textzeilen und Tabellen, die ein Template-Sensor in Home
Assistant beschreibt, gezeichnet vom Bildschirm in seinen eigenen Schriften und Farben. Das Raumklima eines Zimmers auf
einem Tile, eine Liste der Räume, die Akkus, die schwach werden, die nächsten Abfahrten an deiner Haltestelle: alles,
was ein Template sagen kann.

Die Karte richtet sich nach dem Tile, auf dem sie steht. Auf einem Tile, das eine Zeile hoch und zwei oder mehr Spalten
breit ist, stehen die Teile nebeneinander; jedes andere Tile stapelt sie: Werte nebeneinander, ein Balken, eine
Textzeile oder eine Tabellenzeile über die ganze Breite. Werte bekommen die größte Schrift, die passt, auf einem großen
Tile die großen Ziffern der Klimakarte; Tabellen- und Textzeilen wachsen ebenfalls mit dem Platz. Ein Tippen öffnet die
Teile groß auf einer Karte über der Seite, mit ihren Labels.

## Schnellstart, ohne Template

1. Öffne in Tessera **Plugins**, wähle **Eigene Karte** und hake deine Bildschirme an. Jeder Bildschirm baut einmal neu.
2. Platziere im Layout das Tile **Eigene Karte** aus der Gruppe Plugins der Bibliothek und lass seine Entität leer.
3. Wähle im Inspector unter **Wert 1** bis **Wert 6** bis zu sechs Sensoren. Jeder zeigt seinen Wert, seine Einheit,
   seinen Namen und sein Icon (sein eigenes aus Home Assistant, sonst eines für seine Art: Temperatur, Feuchte, CO2,
   Leistung, Akku und mehr, auch an der Einheit erkannt). Ein Wort, das in allen Namen steht („Wohnzimmer“ in
   „Temperatur Wohnzimmer“ und „Wohnzimmer CO2“), steht über der Karte, und die Labels behalten den Rest. **Ampelfarben** färbt CO2, Feuchte und Akkus grün,
   gelb oder rot.

Andere Sensoren zu wählen braucht keinen neuen Build. Für Ringe, Balken, Tabellen, eigene Farben und Bilder nimm ein
Template (unten): Ein Tile, dessen Entität ein Template-Sensor mit `elements` ist, zeigt sein Template und lässt die
sechs Werte weg.

## Einrichten mit Template

1. Lege in Home Assistant einen Template-Sensor an, dessen Attribut `elements` die Teile der Karte aufzählt, einen Text
   je Teil (die Beispiele unten), füge ihn in die `configuration.yaml` ein und lade unter Entwicklerwerkzeuge, YAML die
   **Template-Entitäten** neu.
2. Öffne in Tessera **Plugins**, wähle **Eigene Karte** und hake deine Bildschirme an. Jeder Bildschirm baut einmal neu.
3. Platziere im Layout das Tile **Eigene Karte** aus der Gruppe Plugins der Bibliothek, in jeder Größe, und wähle im
   Inspector den Template-Sensor. Er bietet die Sensoren an, die ein Attribut `elements` haben.

## Beispiele

Kopiere eins, ersetze die Entity-IDs durch deine eigenen und lade die Template-Entitäten neu. Jedes gehört unter
`template:` in der `configuration.yaml`.
[examples/living_room.yaml](https://github.com/StofLE/tessera-plugin-custom-card/blob/main/examples/living_room.yaml)
ist ein größeres Beispiel, mit Stufen für Feuchte und CO2. Jedes Bild zeigt sein Beispiel auf einem 7-Zoll-Screen,
mit ausgedachten Werten. Weitere Rezepte stehen im [Wiki](https://github.com/StofLE/tessera-plugin-custom-card/wiki) (auf Englisch).

### Das Raumklima eines Zimmers

Werte mit Icons, die Farbe der Feuchte nach ihrer Stufe und das CO2 als Balken von 400 bis 2000 ppm.

![Das Raumklima auf einer 2x2-Kachel](docs/examples/climate.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Wohnzimmer-Karte
        state: "{{ states('sensor.wohnzimmer_temperatur') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set t = states('sensor.wohnzimmer_temperatur') %}
            {% set h = states('sensor.wohnzimmer_feuchte') | int(0) %}
            {% set c = states('sensor.wohnzimmer_co2') | int(0) %}
            {{ [
              'value|' ~ t ~ '|°C|Temperatur|blue|thermometer',
              'value|' ~ h ~ '|%|Feuchte|' ~ ('green' if 40 <= h <= 60 else 'orange') ~ '|water-percent',
              'bar|' ~ c ~ '|ppm|CO2|' ~ ('green' if c < 800 else 'yellow' if c < 1200 else 'red')
                ~ '|molecule-co2|400|2000'
            ] }}
```

### Die Luft eines Raums als Ringe

Ringe nebeneinander, jeder gefüllt vom kleinsten bis zum größten Wert, sein Wert groß in seiner Mitte.

![Drei Ringe auf einer 2x2-Kachel](docs/examples/rings.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Luft-Karte
        state: "{{ states('sensor.buero_co2') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set c = states('sensor.buero_co2') | int(0) %}
            {% set h = states('sensor.buero_feuchte') | int(0) %}
            {{ [
              'ring|' ~ c ~ '|ppm|CO2|' ~ ('green' if c < 800 else 'yellow' if c < 1200 else 'red')
                ~ '|molecule-co2|400|2000',
              'ring|' ~ h ~ '|%|Feuchte|' ~ ('green' if 40 <= h <= 60 else 'orange') ~ '|water-percent|0|100',
              'ring|' ~ states('sensor.buero_temperatur') ~ '|°C|Temperatur|blue|thermometer|10|30'
            ] }}
```

### Eine Tabelle der Räume

Aufeinanderfolgende Zeilen stehen als Tabelle: die Namen links, die Werte rechts in einer Spalte.

![Eine Tabelle mit fünf Räumen](docs/examples/rooms.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Räume-Karte
        state: "{{ states('sensor.aussen_temperatur') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set rooms = [
              ('Küche', 'sensor.kueche_temperatur'),
              ('Schlafzimmer', 'sensor.schlafzimmer_temperatur'),
              ('Bad', 'sensor.bad_temperatur'),
              ('Büro', 'sensor.buero_temperatur'),
              ('Außen', 'sensor.aussen_temperatur')] %}
            {% set ns = namespace(rows=[]) %}
            {% for name, entity in rooms %}
              {% set v = states(entity) %}
              {% set v = '-' if v in ['unknown', 'unavailable'] else v %}
              {% set ns.rows = ns.rows + ['row|' ~ v ~ '|°C|' ~ name] %}
            {% endfor %}
            {{ ns.rows[:8] }}
```

### Die Akkus, die schwach werden

Jeder Akku-Sensor im Haus, der schwächste zuerst, rot unter 20 %, gelb unter 50 %. Home Assistant rendert ein Template,
das alle Sensoren durchgeht, höchstens einmal pro Minute; für Akkus reicht das völlig.

![Vier Akkus, der schwächste zuerst](docs/examples/batteries.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Akkus-Karte
        state: "{{ now().minute }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set ns = namespace(items=[]) %}
            {% for s in states.sensor
                 | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
                 | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'eq', 'battery')
                 | rejectattr('state', 'in', ['unknown', 'unavailable']) %}
              {% set ns.items = ns.items + [(s.state | int(0), s.name)] %}
            {% endfor %}
            {% set out = namespace(rows=[]) %}
            {% for level, name in (ns.items | sort(attribute='0'))[:8] %}
              {% set colour = 'red' if level < 20 else 'yellow' if level < 50 else 'green' %}
              {% set out.rows = out.rows + ['row|' ~ level ~ '|%|' ~ name[:18] ~ '|' ~ colour ~ '|battery-high'] %}
            {% endfor %}
            {{ out.rows }}
```

### Abfahrten mit Liniennummer

Ein Kästchen (ein Icon-Feld, das mit `#` beginnt) zeigt die Nummer einer Linie, wie auf einer Abfahrtstafel. Woher die
Liste kommt, hängt von deiner Integration ab; hier ist es ein Attribut `departures` mit `line`, `destination` und
`minutes` je Abfahrt. Ersetze diese Namen durch die deines Sensors.

![Vier Abfahrten mit Linien-Badges](docs/examples/departures.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Abfahrten-Karte
        state: "{{ now().minute }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set ns = namespace(rows=[]) %}
            {% for d in (state_attr('sensor.hauptbahnhof_abfahrten', 'departures') or [])[:8] %}
              {% set when = 'jetzt|' if d.minutes | int(0) == 0 else d.minutes ~ '|min' %}
              {% set ns.rows = ns.rows + ['row|' ~ when ~ '|' ~ d.destination[:18] ~ '|blue|#' ~ d.line] %}
            {% endfor %}
            {{ ns.rows }}
```

### Zählungen mit Anteil und Textzeile

Zwei Zählungen, ihr Anteil als Balken und wann gezählt wurde. Mit `ring` statt `bar` steht der Anteil als Ring neben den
Zählungen, seine Zahl groß darin, so groß, wie die Kachel Platz hat.

![Zwei Zählungen, ein Balken und eine Textzeile](docs/examples/counts.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Einlass-Karte
        state: "{{ states('sensor.einlass_gescannt') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set s = states('sensor.einlass_gescannt') | int(0) %}
            {% set v = states('sensor.einlass_gueltig') | int(0) %}
            {% set p = (100 * s / v) | round(0) | int if v else 0 %}
            {{ [
              'value|' ~ s ~ '||Gescannt',
              'value|' ~ v ~ '||Gültig',
              'bar|' ~ p ~ '|%|Anteil|blue||0|100',
              'text|Stand ' ~ states('sensor.einlass_uhrzeit') ~ '||||clock-outline'
            ] }}
```

### Zählungen größer als die Ziffern des Screens

Dieselben Zählungen als Bilder: Ein `image`-Teil steht, wo sonst ein Wert stünde, und wächst in den Platz der Kachel,
so sind zwei Zählungen auf einer breiten Kachel (3x2, 4x2) etwa doppelt so hoch wie die größten Ziffern des Screens.
Das Bild muss jemand zeichnen: Hier holt es ein Template-Image von einem kleinen Dienst im Haus, der eine Zahl zeichnet
([examples/value-image](examples/value-image)); jede Bild-Entität geht genauso. Die Zählung ist die Marke des Teils:
Ändert sie sich, ist die Adresse des Bildes neu, und wo es keine Bilder gibt, steht sie als Wert. Läuft bei dir die
AppDaemon-App in Home Assistant? Das [Wiki](https://github.com/StofLE/tessera-plugin-custom-card/wiki/Numbers-as-pictures-with-AppDaemon) hat ein Rezept, das die Zahlen
dort zeichnet, ohne eigene Maschine (auf Englisch).

![Zwei Zählungen als Bilder auf einer 4x2-Kachel](docs/examples/counts-image.png)

```yaml
template:
  - image:
      - name: Zählung gescannt
        default_entity_id: image.zaehlung_gescannt
        verify_ssl: false
        url: "http://192.168.1.20:8765/value.png?ink=300&text={{ states('sensor.einlass_gescannt') | int(0) }}"
      - name: Zählung gültig
        default_entity_id: image.zaehlung_gueltig
        verify_ssl: false
        url: "http://192.168.1.20:8765/value.png?ink=300&text={{ states('sensor.einlass_gueltig') | int(0) }}"
  - sensor:
      - name: Einlass-Karte
        state: "{{ states('sensor.einlass_gescannt') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set s = states('sensor.einlass_gescannt') | int(0) %}
            {% set v = states('sensor.einlass_gueltig') | int(0) %}
            {{ [
              'image|' ~ s ~ '|zaehlung_gescannt|Gescannt',
              'image|' ~ v ~ '|zaehlung_gueltig|Gültig',
              'bar|' ~ ((100 * s / v) | round(0) | int if v else 0) ~ '|%|Anteil|blue||0|100'
            ] }}
```

## Die Teile

Jeder Teil ist ein Text, seine Felder durch `|` getrennt in dieser Reihenfolge: Art, Wert, Einheit, Label, Farbe, Icon
und bei einem Balken oder Ring sein kleinster und größter Wert. Felder am Ende dürfen fehlen; ein Feld in der Mitte bleibt leer
(`value|3||Offen`).

| Art | Was sie zeigt | Beispiel |
|---|---|---|
| `value` | Eine Zahl oder ein Wort mit Einheit, Label und Icon darüber. | `value\|21,4\|°C\|Temperatur\|blue\|thermometer` |
| `bar` | Eine Zahl mit einem Balken darunter, vom kleinsten bis zum größten Wert (ohne Angabe 0 und 100). | `bar\|820\|ppm\|CO2\|yellow\|molecule-co2\|400\|2000` |
| `text` | Eine Textzeile; eine lange nimmt zwei Zeilen, wo die Karte Platz hat. | `text\|Tür offen\|\|\|\|door-open` |
| `row` | Eine Zeile einer Tabelle: das Label links, der Wert rechts. Aufeinanderfolgende Zeilen stehen als Tabelle. | `row\|20,8\|°C\|Küche` |
| `ring` | Ein Ring, gefüllt vom kleinsten bis zum größten Wert (ohne Angabe 0 und 100), der Wert in seiner Mitte, Icon und Label darunter. Aufeinanderfolgende Ringe stehen nebeneinander, alle so groß wie der größte; neben Werten ist es derselbe Ring, er steht zwischen ihnen und wächst in den Platz der Kachel; wo sie nicht passen, steht die Zahl als Wert. | `ring\|46\|%\|Feuchte\|green\|water-percent\|0\|100` |
| `image` | Ein Bild von Home Assistant, wo sonst ein Wert stünde, links unter seinem Label: Seine Felder sind Marke, Quelle, Label, Farbe, Icon und Fit. Die Quelle ist eine Bild-Entität ohne `image.` oder ein Pfad, der mit `/` beginnt; die Marke ändert sich mit dem Bild und steht als Wert, wo es keine Bilder gibt. `contain` (Standard) zeigt das ganze Bild, `cover` füllt seinen Platz. | `image\|5358\|zaehlung_gescannt\|Gescannt` |

- **Farbe**: `red`, `orange`, `yellow`, `green`, `mint`, `blue`, `purple`, `pink` oder `gray`. Wie auf Tesseras eigenen
  Tiles markiert sie einen Teil: Sie färbt das Icon (einen Punkt, wo der Teil keins hat), den Balken, den Ring und ein
  Kästchen, die Schrift bleibt in den Farben des Looks. Die Option **Werte in ihrer Farbe** der Kachel färbt auch die
  Zahlen. `green` gut, `yellow` und `orange` mäßig, `red` schlecht und `blue` die Akzentfarbe sind Tesseras eigene
  Farben, hell und dunkel gut lesbar.
- **Icon**: ein Name aus der Icon-Auswahl des Editors, mit oder ohne `mdi:`.
- **Kästchen**: Ein Icon-Feld, das mit `#` beginnt, zeigt den Text danach in einem Kästchen in der Farbe des Teils (ohne
  Farbe in der Akzentfarbe), etwa die Nummer einer Linie: `row|4|min|Hauptbahnhof|blue|#16`. Höchstens 8 Zeichen.

## Gut zu wissen

- Home Assistant rendert das Template; das Tile ändert sich, sobald sich der Sensor ändert. Stufen und Farben berechnest
  du im Template, dort rundest du die Werte und wählst das Dezimalzeichen.
- Höchstens acht Teile (zwei Reihen mit vier Werten), jeder höchstens 48 Bytes: Tessera kürzt längere Texte, also Labels
  kurz halten (die Beispiele kürzen Namen mit `[:18]`). Es zählt die ganze Zeile mit jedem `|`, ein Umlaut zählt doppelt.
  Das Icon steht am Ende und geht deshalb als Erstes verloren: `value|Zu||Untergeschoss|green|window-closed-variant`
  (51 Bytes) zeigt einen Punkt statt des Icons, `value|Zu||UG|green|window-closed-variant` (40 Bytes) das Icon.
- Ist ein Tile zu klein für alle Teile, stehen die Werte zu zweit oder einzeln in einer Reihe, und es erscheinen die
  Zeilen, die ganz passen: keine Zahl wird abgeschnitten, keine Zeile halbiert. Ein Text neben anderen Teilen auf einem
  flachen Tile bleibt ganz, wo die Teile stattdessen untereinander stehen können.
- Die Schrift eines Werts richtet sich nach seiner Form, nicht nach den Ziffern, so behält das Tile seine Größe, wenn
  sich ein Wert ändert.
- Ein `image` zeigt sein Bild auf dem Tile und auf der Karte, die ein Tippen öffnet, auf einem Board mit Speicher für
  Bilder (nicht CYD, Waveshare 3.5 Zoll und Hosyond 4 Zoll); dort steht seine Marke als Wert. Wo sein Bild nicht kommt
  (Home Assistant hat unter der Adresse keins, oder der Download brach ab), steht seine Marke ebenfalls als Wert, bis
  sich die Marke ändert. Tesseras App holt das Bild mit ihrem eigenen Zugang, nur von Home Assistant, und fragt erneut,
  wenn sich die Marke ändert. Mehrere Bilder einer
  Karte sind für den Screen ein Bild, das ganz neu kommt, wenn sich eines davon ändert.
- Ist der Sensor eine Weile nicht verfügbar, behält das Tile ihn und zeigt seinen Zustand, bis `elements` wieder da ist.
- Ein Plugin-Tile kann keine ganze Seite belegen; jede andere Größe des Rasters geht.
- Die Hintergrundfarbe des Tiles stellst du im Editor ein, wie bei jedem Tile. Sein Inspector hat drei eigene
  Optionen: **Namen zeigen** (an) für den Namen über den Teilen (aus gibt den Teilen seinen Platz), **Werte in ihrer
  Farbe** (aus), um auch jede Zahl in der Farbe ihres Teils zu zeigen, hell und dunkel lesbar, und **Werte in einer
  Reihe** (automatisch): alle Werte und Ringe in einer Reihe oder zu zweit, statt der Anordnung, in der sie am größten
  werden (vier Werte auf einer breiten Kachel als eine Reihe mit vier oder zwei Reihen mit zwei). Die Karte, die ein
  Tippen öffnet, zeigt ihre Zahlen weiter in der normalen Schriftfarbe und wählt ihre Anordnung selbst.

## Wie es funktioniert

- `tessera-plugin.yaml`: ein Tile, das zu einem Sensor gehört und dessen `elements` und `unit_of_measurement` bekommt.
- `components/custom_card/`: die ESPHome-Komponente, die die Teile anordnet und zeichnet, auf dem Tile und auf der
  Karte, die ein Tippen öffnet.
- `translations/`: die Texte auf dem Bildschirm (`screen`) und in der App (`app`).
- `CHANGELOG.de.md`: was jede Version geändert hat; die App zeigt es bei einem Update.
- `tools/make_icons.py`: schreibt die Namen von Tesseras Icon-Satz in `icons.h`.
readme.en:
# Custom card

A tile you put together yourself: values, rings, bars, lines of words and tables that a template sensor in Home
Assistant describes, drawn by the screen in its own fonts and colours. A room's climate on one tile, a list of rooms,
the batteries that run low, the next departures from your stop: whatever a template can say.

The card lays itself out for the tile it stands on. On a tile one row high and two columns or more the parts stand side
by side; any other tile stacks them: values side by side, a bar, a line of words or a row of a table across the width.
Values take the largest face that fits, on a large tile the climate card's large digits; rows and words grow with the
room as well. A tap opens the parts large on a card over the page, with their labels.

## Quick start, without a template

1. In Tessera, open **Plugins**, choose **Custom card** and tick your screens. Each screen builds once.
2. In Layout, place the **Custom card** tile from the library's Plugins group and leave its entity empty.
3. Pick up to six sensors under **Value 1** to **Value 6** in its inspector. Each shows its value, its unit, its name
   and its icon (its own from Home Assistant, else one for its kind or its unit: temperature, humidity, CO2, power, a
   battery and more). A word all the names share ("Living room" of "Living room Temperature" and "Humidity living
   room") heads the card, and the labels keep the rest. **Traffic lights** colours CO2, humidity and batteries green, yellow or red.

Choosing other sensors needs no new build. For rings, bars, tables, colours of your own and pictures, use a template
(below): a tile whose entity is a template sensor with `elements` shows its template and leaves the six values out.

## Set up with a template

1. In Home Assistant, make a template sensor whose attribute `elements` lists the card's parts, one text per part (the
   examples below), put it in `configuration.yaml`, and reload **Template entities** in Developer tools, YAML.
2. In Tessera, open **Plugins**, choose **Custom card** and tick your screens. Each screen builds once.
3. In Layout, place the **Custom card** tile from the library's Plugins group, at any size, and choose the template
   sensor in its inspector. It offers the sensors that have an `elements` attribute.

## Examples

Copy one, change the entity ids to your own, and reload Template entities. Each goes under `template:` in
`configuration.yaml`.
[examples/living_room.yaml](https://github.com/StofLE/tessera-plugin-custom-card/blob/main/examples/living_room.yaml)
is a larger one, with levels for the humidity and the CO2. Each picture shows its example on a 7-inch screen, with
made-up values. More recipes are in the [wiki](https://github.com/StofLE/tessera-plugin-custom-card/wiki).

### A room's climate

Values with icons, the humidity's colour by its level, and the CO2 as a bar from 400 to 2000 ppm.

![A room's climate on a 2x2 tile](docs/examples/climate.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Living room card
        state: "{{ states('sensor.living_room_temperature') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set t = states('sensor.living_room_temperature') %}
            {% set h = states('sensor.living_room_humidity') | int(0) %}
            {% set c = states('sensor.living_room_co2') | int(0) %}
            {{ [
              'value|' ~ t ~ '|°C|Temperature|blue|thermometer',
              'value|' ~ h ~ '|%|Humidity|' ~ ('green' if 40 <= h <= 60 else 'orange') ~ '|water-percent',
              'bar|' ~ c ~ '|ppm|CO2|' ~ ('green' if c < 800 else 'yellow' if c < 1200 else 'red')
                ~ '|molecule-co2|400|2000'
            ] }}
```

### The air of a room as rings

Rings side by side, each filled from its lowest to its highest value, its value large in its middle.

![Three rings on a 2x2 tile](docs/examples/rings.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Air card
        state: "{{ states('sensor.office_co2') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set c = states('sensor.office_co2') | int(0) %}
            {% set h = states('sensor.office_humidity') | int(0) %}
            {{ [
              'ring|' ~ c ~ '|ppm|CO2|' ~ ('green' if c < 800 else 'yellow' if c < 1200 else 'red')
                ~ '|molecule-co2|400|2000',
              'ring|' ~ h ~ '|%|Humidity|' ~ ('green' if 40 <= h <= 60 else 'orange') ~ '|water-percent|0|100',
              'ring|' ~ states('sensor.office_temperature') ~ '|°C|Temperature|blue|thermometer|10|30'
            ] }}
```

### A table of rooms

Rows that follow each other stand as a table: the names at the left, the values in one column at the right.

![A table of five rooms](docs/examples/rooms.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Rooms card
        state: "{{ states('sensor.outside_temperature') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set rooms = [
              ('Kitchen', 'sensor.kitchen_temperature'),
              ('Bedroom', 'sensor.bedroom_temperature'),
              ('Bath', 'sensor.bath_temperature'),
              ('Office', 'sensor.office_temperature'),
              ('Outside', 'sensor.outside_temperature')] %}
            {% set ns = namespace(rows=[]) %}
            {% for name, entity in rooms %}
              {% set v = states(entity) %}
              {% set v = '-' if v in ['unknown', 'unavailable'] else v %}
              {% set ns.rows = ns.rows + ['row|' ~ v ~ '|°C|' ~ name] %}
            {% endfor %}
            {{ ns.rows[:8] }}
```

### The batteries that run low

Every battery sensor of the house, the lowest first, red under 20 %, yellow under 50 %. Home Assistant renders a
template that walks all sensors at most once a minute, which is plenty for batteries.

![Four batteries, the lowest first](docs/examples/batteries.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Batteries card
        state: "{{ now().minute }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set ns = namespace(items=[]) %}
            {% for s in states.sensor
                 | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'defined')
                 | selectattr('attributes.device_class', 'eq', 'battery')
                 | rejectattr('state', 'in', ['unknown', 'unavailable']) %}
              {% set ns.items = ns.items + [(s.state | int(0), s.name)] %}
            {% endfor %}
            {% set out = namespace(rows=[]) %}
            {% for level, name in (ns.items | sort(attribute='0'))[:8] %}
              {% set colour = 'red' if level < 20 else 'yellow' if level < 50 else 'green' %}
              {% set out.rows = out.rows + ['row|' ~ level ~ '|%|' ~ name[:18] ~ '|' ~ colour ~ '|battery-high'] %}
            {% endfor %}
            {{ out.rows }}
```

### Departures with the line's number

A badge (an icon field that starts with `#`) shows a line's number in a box, as on a departure board. Where the list
comes from depends on your integration; here it is an attribute `departures` with `line`, `destination` and `minutes`
for each, so change those names to what your sensor has.

![Four departures with line badges](docs/examples/departures.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Departures card
        state: "{{ now().minute }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set ns = namespace(rows=[]) %}
            {% for d in (state_attr('sensor.main_station_departures', 'departures') or [])[:8] %}
              {% set when = 'now|' if d.minutes | int(0) == 0 else d.minutes ~ '|min' %}
              {% set ns.rows = ns.rows + ['row|' ~ when ~ '|' ~ d.destination[:18] ~ '|blue|#' ~ d.line] %}
            {% endfor %}
            {{ ns.rows }}
```

### Counts with a share and a line of words

Two counts, their share as a bar, and when they were counted. With `ring` instead of `bar` the share stands beside the
counts as a ring with its number large inside, as large as the tile has room for.

![Two counts, a bar and a line of words](docs/examples/counts.png)

```yaml
template:
  - sensor:
      - name: Entrance card
        state: "{{ states('sensor.entrance_scanned') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set s = states('sensor.entrance_scanned') | int(0) %}
            {% set v = states('sensor.entrance_valid') | int(0) %}
            {% set p = (100 * s / v) | round(0) | int if v else 0 %}
            {{ [
              'value|' ~ s ~ '||Scanned',
              'value|' ~ v ~ '||Valid',
              'bar|' ~ p ~ '|%|Share|blue||0|100',
              'text|Counted at ' ~ states('sensor.entrance_time') ~ '||||clock-outline'
            ] }}
```

### Counts larger than the screen's digits

The same counts as pictures: an `image` part stands where a value would and grows into the room the tile has, so on a
wide tile (3x2, 4x2) two counts are about twice as tall as the screen's largest digits. Something has to draw the
picture: here a template image fetches it from a small service in the house that draws a number
([examples/value-image](examples/value-image)); any image entity works the same way. The count is the part's mark: it
makes the address new when it changes, and it stands as a value where there are no pictures. Running the AppDaemon
app in Home Assistant? The [wiki](https://github.com/StofLE/tessera-plugin-custom-card/wiki/Numbers-as-pictures-with-AppDaemon) has a recipe that draws the numbers there,
with no extra machine.

![Two counts drawn as pictures on a 4x2 tile](docs/examples/counts-image.png)

```yaml
template:
  - image:
      - name: Count scanned
        default_entity_id: image.count_scanned
        verify_ssl: false
        url: "http://192.168.1.20:8765/value.png?ink=300&text={{ states('sensor.entrance_scanned') | int(0) }}"
      - name: Count valid
        default_entity_id: image.count_valid
        verify_ssl: false
        url: "http://192.168.1.20:8765/value.png?ink=300&text={{ states('sensor.entrance_valid') | int(0) }}"
  - sensor:
      - name: Entrance card
        state: "{{ states('sensor.entrance_scanned') }}"
        attributes:
          elements: >
            {% set s = states('sensor.entrance_scanned') | int(0) %}
            {% set v = states('sensor.entrance_valid') | int(0) %}
            {{ [
              'image|' ~ s ~ '|count_scanned|Scanned',
              'image|' ~ v ~ '|count_valid|Valid',
              'bar|' ~ ((100 * s / v) | round(0) | int if v else 0) ~ '|%|Share|blue||0|100'
            ] }}
```

## The parts

Each part is one text, its fields split by `|` in this order: kind, value, unit, label, colour, icon, and for a bar or
a ring its lowest and highest value. Fields at the end may be left out; a field in the middle stays empty (`value|3||Open`).

| Kind | What it shows | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `value` | A number or a word with its unit, the label and icon above it. | `value\|21.4\|°C\|Temperature\|blue\|thermometer` |
| `bar` | A number with a bar under it, from its lowest to its highest value (0 and 100 when left out). | `bar\|820\|ppm\|CO2\|yellow\|molecule-co2\|400\|2000` |
| `text` | A line of words; a long one takes two lines where the card has room. | `text\|Door open\|\|\|\|door-open` |
| `row` | A row of a table: its label at the left, its value at the right. Rows that follow each other stand as a table. | `row\|20.8\|°C\|Kitchen` |
| `ring` | A ring filled from its lowest to its highest value (0 and 100 when left out), the value in its middle, the icon and the label under it. Rings that follow each other stand side by side, all as large as the largest; beside values a ring is the same ring and stands among them, growing into the room the tile has; where they do not fit, the number stands as a value. | `ring\|46\|%\|Humidity\|green\|water-percent\|0\|100` |
| `image` | A picture of Home Assistant's own where a value would stand, from the left under its label: its fields are the mark, the source, the label, the colour, the icon and the fit. The source is an image entity without `image.` or a path that starts with `/`; the mark changes with the picture and stands as a value where there are no pictures. `contain` (the default) shows the whole picture, `cover` fills its place. | `image\|5358\|count_scanned\|Scanned` |

- **Colour**: `red`, `orange`, `yellow`, `green`, `mint`, `blue`, `purple`, `pink` or `gray`. As on Tessera's own tiles
  it marks a part: it colours the icon (a dot where the part has none), the bar, the ring and a badge, and the words
  stay in the look's own colours. The tile's option **Values in their colour** paints the numbers too. `green` good,
  `yellow` and `orange` moderate, `red` bad and `blue` the accent are Tessera's own colours, readable in light and
  dark.
- **Icon**: a name from the editor's icon picker, with or without `mdi:`.
- **Badge**: an icon field that starts with `#` shows the words after it in a box of the part's colour (the accent
  without one), such as a line's number: `row|4|min|Main station|blue|#16`. At most 8 characters.

## Good to know

- Home Assistant renders the template; the tile changes whenever the sensor does. Work out levels and colours in the
  template, round values there, and write the decimal sign you want.
- At most eight parts (two rows of four values), each at most 48 bytes: Tessera cuts longer texts, so keep labels short
  (the examples cut names with `[:18]`). The whole line counts, every `|` with it, and an umlaut counts twice. The icon
  comes last, so it is the first to go: `value|Closed||Basement|green|window-closed-variant` (50 bytes) shows a dot
  instead of its icon, `value|Closed||Base|green|window-closed-variant` (46 bytes) shows the icon.
- Where a tile is too small for every part, the values stand two to a row, or one, and the lines that fit whole show:
  no number is cut short and no line cut in half. A text beside other parts on a flat tile stays whole where the parts
  can stand under each other instead.
- The face of a value is chosen for its shape, not its digits, so the tile keeps its size when a value ticks.
- An `image` shows its picture on the tile and on the card a tap opens, on a board with the memory for pictures (not
  the CYD, the Waveshare 3.5-inch or the Hosyond 4-inch); there its mark stands as a value. Where its picture does not
  come (Home Assistant has none at that address, or the download broke off), its mark stands as a value too, until the
  mark changes. Tessera's app fetches the picture with its own access, only from Home Assistant, and asks again when
  the mark changes. Several images on a
  card are one picture for the screen, sent again whole when one of them changes.
- When the sensor is unavailable for a while, the tile keeps it and shows its state until `elements` is back.
- A plugin tile cannot take a whole page; any other size of the grid is fine.
- The tile's background colour is set in the editor, as for every tile. Its inspector has three options of its own:
  **Show the name** (on) for the tile's name over the parts (off gives the parts its room), **Values in their
  colour** (off) to paint each number in its part's colour as well, readable in light and dark, and **Values in a row**
  (automatic): all values and rings in one row, or two to a row, instead of the arrangement that makes them largest
  (four values on a wide tile as one row of four or two rows of two). The card a tap opens keeps its numbers in the
  look's ink and chooses its arrangement itself.

## How it works

- `tessera-plugin.yaml`: one tile that belongs to a sensor and gets its `elements` and `unit_of_measurement`.
- `components/custom_card/`: the ESPHome component that lays the parts out and draws them, on the tile and on the
  card a tap opens.
- `translations/`: the words on the screen (`screen`) and in the app (`app`).
- `CHANGELOG.md`: what each version changed; the app shows it with an update.
- `tools/make_icons.py`: writes the names of Tessera's icon set into `icons.h`.

changelog.de:
# Änderungen

## 0.8.0 - 2026-10-30
- Eine Karte ohne Template: Wähle im Inspector der Kachel unter Wert 1 bis Wert 6 bis zu sechs Sensoren (Plugin-API
  0.15). Jeder zeigt seinen Wert mit Einheit, seinen Namen und sein Icon, sein eigenes oder eines für seine Art von
  Sensor (seine Geräteklasse, bei einem Sensor ohne sie seine Einheit, ppm als CO2). Die Wörter, die in allen Namen
  stehen, stehen über der Karte, egal an welcher Stelle, die Labels behalten den Rest. Eine Zahl mit mehr als einer
  Nachkommastelle zeigt eine (ab 100 keine), mit dem Dezimalzeichen des Screens. Die Option Ampelfarben färbt CO2 (bis
  1000 ppm grün, bis 1400 gelb), Feuchte (40 bis 60 % grün, 30 bis 70 % gelb) und Akkus (über 50 % grün, über 20 %
  gelb), darüber hinaus rot. Andere Sensoren brauchen keinen neuen Build. Ein Tile, dessen Entität ein Template-Sensor
  mit `elements` ist, behält sein Template und lässt die sechs Werte weg. Die README beginnt mit diesem Schnellstart.
- Die README verweist auf die Rezepte im Wiki, darunter Zahlen als Bilder, gezeichnet von AppDaemon.
- Ein Bild, das nicht kommt (Home Assistant hat unter der Adresse keins, oder der Download brach ab), zeigt seine Marke
  als Wert statt eines leeren grauen Blocks, bis sich die Marke ändert oder das Bild doch noch kommt (Plugin-API 0.17,
  on_picture). Gesehen, als der Dienst, der eine Zählung zeichnet, eine Weile nicht erreichbar war.
- Braucht Tessera 0.4.91 oder neuer (Plugin-API 0.17).

## 0.7.0 - 2026-10-23
- Ein neuer Teil, `image`: ein Bild von Home Assistant, wo sonst ein Wert stünde, etwa eine Zählung, die ein Template
  größer gezeichnet hat als die größten Ziffern des Screens, das Plakat einer Veranstaltung oder das Foto einer Person:
  `image|<Marke>|<Quelle>|<Label>|<Farbe>|<Icon>|<Fit>`. Die Quelle ist eine Bild-Entität ohne ihr `image.`
  (`image|5.358|zaehler_gescannt|Gescannt`) oder ein Pfad von Home Assistant (`/local/plakat.jpg`); die Marke ändert
  sich mit dem Bild, und wo es keine Bilder gibt (ein Board ohne Speicher dafür), zeigt die Karte sie als Wert. Die
  Karte nach einem Tipp zeigt die Bilder ebenfalls, größer in ihrem Platz. Bilder stehen nebeneinander wie Werte, links
  unter ihren Labels, und nehmen den Platz, den die Kachel übrig hat, bis sie ihre Spalten füllen. `contain` (Standard)
  zeigt das ganze Bild auf der Farbe der Karte, `cover` füllt seinen Platz.
- Die README zeigt zu jedem Beispiel ein Bild auf einem Screen, so lässt sich jede Zeile eines Templates dem zuordnen,
  was sie zeichnet (Issue #6), und sagt, dass die ganze Zeile eines Teils zu seinen 48 Bytes zählt, eine lange also
  zuerst ihr Icon verliert.
- Braucht Tessera 0.4.89 oder neuer (Plugin-API 0.13, Bilder auf einer Karte).

## 0.6.1 - 2026-10-18
- Ringe so groß wie die Kachel: Auf einer Karte mit Ringen wachsen sie in den Platz, den die Kachel hat (so hoch wie
  eine breite Kachel mit einer Reihe), alle gleich groß, ihre Werte in der größten Schrift, die die Ringe fassen, und
  das Label steht in der offenen Unterseite seines Rings statt darunter.
- Vier Werte auf einer breiten Kachel mit einer Reihe stehen als zwei Reihen zu zwei, wo sie dadurch größer werden als
  in einer Reihe.
- Werte, deren Teile alle ein Icon haben, nehmen die Zeile der Labels, wo sie dadurch größer werden: Das Icon rückt zu
  seinem Label, so hat jeder Wert die ganze Breite seiner Spalte (vier Werte in einer Reihe unter dem Namen der Kachel).
- Eine dritte Option der Kachel im Inspector: **Werte in einer Reihe**, automatisch (wie bisher), alle in einer Reihe
  oder zwei pro Reihe (vier Werte auf einer breiten Kachel als eine Reihe mit vier oder zwei Reihen mit zwei).
- Diese vier von Schumey (Pull Request #3), danke.
- Ein Ring, wo er auch steht: Ein Ring zwischen Werten (zwei Zählungen und ihr Anteil) ist derselbe Ring wie auf einer
  Karte mit Ringen, sein Wert groß in der Mitte, sein Label in der Öffnung, und er wächst in den Platz der Kachel,
  höchstens anderthalbmal so hoch wie die Zeile der Werte, damit er auf großen Kacheln zu ihnen passt; die Werte daneben
  stehen in der Mitte der Zeile. Der kleine Ring, so hoch wie die Zahlen der Werte, entfällt.
- Ein Ring zwischen Werten kommt nie allein in eine eigene Reihe: Wo eine schmale Kachel neben ihnen keinen Platz für ihn
  hat, steht sein Anteil als Wert unter den Zählungen, die ihre große Schrift behalten.
- Ringe, die nur ohne den Namen der Kachel passen, weichen ihren Zahlen als Werte, wo diese ihn behalten: Eine 2x1-Kachel
  mit Ringen zeigt ihren Namen.

## 0.6.0 - 2026-10-17
- Eine Tabelle: aufeinanderfolgende `row`-Teile stehen als Zeilen, das Label links und der Wert rechts, so stehen die
  Werte einer Liste (Räume, Akkus, Abfahrten) untereinander.
- Eine lange Textzeile nimmt zwei Zeilen, wo die Karte Platz hat, statt mit Punkten zu enden.
- Tabellen- und Textzeilen bekommen eine größere Schrift, wo die Karte Platz hat, nie größer als ihre Werte.
- Ein Ring: `ring`-Teile stehen als Ringe, mehrere nebeneinander (die Luft eines Raums, die Akkus im Haus), der Wert
  groß in der Mitte seines Rings, Icon und Label darunter, alle Ringe einer Reihe so groß wie der größte (Schumeys
  Entwurf, Pull Request #2). Ein Ring behält Icon und Label darunter immer, auch wo Werte ihre für eine größere Schrift
  aufgeben: Seine Farbe sagt, wie gut ein Wert ist, nicht, was er ist. Auf einer Karte mit Werten ist ein Ring kompakt: Er steht zwischen ihnen, so hoch wie ihre Zahlen, mit
  seiner Zahl innen (ein Anteil neben zwei Zählungen). Auf einem zu kleinen Tile stehen ihre Zahlen als Werte.
- Ein Kästchen: Ein Icon-Feld, das mit `#` beginnt, zeigt seinen Text in einem Kästchen in der Farbe des Teils, wie die
  Liniennummer in einer Abfahrtsliste (`row|4|min|Hauptbahnhof|blue|#16`).
- Die Werte einer kürzeren Reihe stehen unter den Spalten der Reihe darüber, statt sich über die Breite zu verteilen.
- Die Karte hält ihre Teile im PSRAM des Bildschirms, so bleibt der Speicher frei, den das WLAN braucht.
- Werte bekommen die großen Ziffern auch neben einer Zeile mit Uhrzeit oder Worten (`row|15:25||Renntag`): Es zählen nur
  die Werte, die groß stehen, so sind zwei Zahlen über einem Anteil und einer Uhrzeit so groß, wie die Karte es zulässt.
- Zwei Optionen der Kachel im Inspector (Schumey, Pull Request #2): **Namen zeigen** (an) und **Werte in ihrer Farbe**
  (aus). Beide lassen eine Kachel standardmäßig so, wie sie war.
- Braucht Tessera 0.4.88 oder neuer.

## 0.5.0 - 2026-10-14
- Große Zahlen auf großen Tiles: Wo sie passen und alle Werte Zahlen sind, bekommen die Werte die großen Ziffern
  der Klimakarte von Tessera. Ein Wert mit einem Wort darin behält seine bisherige Schrift.
- Grün, Gelb, Orange, Rot und Blau sind Tesseras eigene Farben nach Bedeutung (gut, mäßig, schlecht, Akzent), hell und
  dunkel auf der Karte lesbar, wie Tessera einen Wert einfärbt.
- Wo auf einer kleinen Kachel nichts passt, stehen die Werte zu zweit oder einzeln untereinander, statt in einer Zeile
  abgeschnitten zu werden.
- Ein Text neben anderen Teilen auf einer flachen Kachel bleibt ganz, wo die Teile stattdessen untereinander stehen
  können; Labels gehen weiterhin vor.
- Braucht Tessera 0.4.88 oder neuer: eine ältere bietet weiter 0.4.3 an.

## 0.4.3 - 2026-10-12
- Bis zu acht Teile auf einer Karte statt sechs: zwei volle Reihen mit vier Werten. Jede Kachel der Karte kostet den
  Bildschirm dafür etwas mehr Speicher.
- Textzeilen und Balken über die ganze Breite werden auf einer niedrigen Kachel mit den Werten kleiner, statt unten
  herauszulaufen; wo selbst die kleinste Größe zu groß ist, zeigt die Karte die Zeilen, die ganz passen.

## 0.4.2 - 2026-10-12
- Ein Bild auf der Plugins-Seite.

## 0.4.1 - 2026-10-11
- Ein farbiges Icon wird im hellen Modus dunkler, wo es sich sonst nicht von der Karte abhebt: ein gelbes wird auf Weiß ocker.

## 0.4.0 - 2026-10-10
- Ein Tippen auf das Tile öffnet die Teile groß auf einer Karte über der Seite, mit ihren Labels.
- Braucht ein Tessera vom 10.10.2026 oder neuer: ein älteres zeigt die Karte unter ihrer Titelzeile leer.

## 0.3.3 - 2026-10-09
- Auf der Plugins-Seite unter dem Thema Zuhause zu finden.
- Braucht ein Tessera mit Plugin-API 0.7: erst die App aktualisieren.

## 0.3.2 - 2026-10-09
- Ein Label ohne Icon und ohne Farbe bleibt immer, so sagt jede Zahl, was sie ist.
- Ein Icon oder Punkt vor einer Zahl hat etwas mehr Abstand zu ihr.

## 0.3.1 - 2026-10-09
- Der Inspector des Tiles bietet nur noch Sensoren an, die eine Karte beschreiben (mit einem Attribut `elements`).

## 0.3.0 - 2026-10-09
- Erste Version: Werte, Balken und Textzeilen, die ein Template-Sensor beschreibt, nebeneinander auf einem breiten
  Tile und gestapelt auf jedem anderen, in den Schriften und Farben des Bildschirms.
changelog.en:
# Changelog

## 0.8.0 - 2026-10-30
- A card without a template: pick up to six sensors under Value 1 to Value 6 in the tile's inspector (plugin API
  0.15). Each shows its value with its unit, its name and its icon, its own or one for its kind of sensor (its device
  class, or its unit for a sensor without one, ppm as CO2). The words all their names share head the card, wherever they
  stand, and the labels keep the rest. A number with more than one decimal shows one (none from 100 on), with the
  screen's decimal mark. The option Traffic lights colours CO2 (up to 1000 ppm green, up to
  1400 yellow), humidity (40 to 60 % green, 30 to 70 % yellow) and batteries (over 50 % green, over 20 % yellow) and
  red beyond. Other sensors need no new build. A tile whose entity is a template sensor with `elements` keeps its
  template and leaves the six values out. The README starts with this quick start.
- The README points to the wiki's recipes, among them numbers as pictures drawn by AppDaemon.
- An image whose picture does not come (Home Assistant has none at that address, or the download broke off) shows its
  mark as a value instead of an empty grey block, until the mark changes or the picture comes after all (plugin API
  0.17, on_picture). Seen when the service that draws a count was not reachable for a while.
- Needs Tessera 0.4.91 or later (plugin API 0.17).

## 0.7.0 - 2026-10-23
- A new part, `image`: a picture of Home Assistant's own where a value would stand, such as a count a template drew
  larger than the screen's largest digits, an event's poster or a person's photo:
  `image|<mark>|<source>|<label>|<colour>|<icon>|<fit>`. The source is an image entity without its `image.`
  (`image|5.358|counter_scanned|Scanned`) or a path of Home Assistant's own (`/local/poster.jpg`); the mark changes with
  the picture, and where there are no pictures (a board without the memory for them) the card shows it as a value. The
  card a tap opens shows the pictures too, larger in its room. Images stand side by side as values do, from the left
  under their labels, and take the room the tile has left until they fill their columns. `contain` (the default) shows
  the whole picture on the card's colour, `cover` fills its place.
- The README shows a picture of every example on a screen, so each line of a template can be matched to what it draws
  (issue #6), and says that a part's whole line counts towards its 48 bytes, so a long one loses its icon first.
- Needs Tessera 0.4.89 or later (plugin API 0.13, pictures on a card).

## 0.6.1 - 2026-10-18
- Rings as large as the tile: on a card of rings they grow into the room the tile has (as tall as a wide tile one row
  high), all of one size, their values in the largest face the rings hold, and the label stands in the open bottom of
  its ring instead of under it.
- Four values on a wide tile one row high stand as two rows of two where that gives them a larger face than one row.
- Values whose parts all have an icon take the row of labels where it makes them larger: the icon moves up to its
  label, so each value has its column's whole width (four values in one row under the tile's name).
- A third option of the tile in the inspector: **Values in a row**, automatic (as before), all in one row, or two to a
  row (four values on a wide tile as one row of four or two rows of two).
- These four by Schumey (pull request #3), thank you.
- One ring wherever it stands: a ring among values (two counts and their share) is the same ring as on a card of rings,
  its value large in its middle and its label in its opening, and it grows into the room the tile has, at most half
  again as tall as the values' line so it stays in step with them on a large tile, with the values in the middle of the
  line beside it. The small ring as tall as the values' numbers is gone.
- A ring among values is never set apart on a row of its own: where a narrow tile has no room for it beside them, its
  share stands as a value under the counts, which keep their large face.
- Rings that fit only without the tile's name give way to their numbers as values where those keep it: a 2x1 of rings
  shows its name.

## 0.6.0 - 2026-10-17
- A table: `row` parts that follow each other stand as rows, each label at the left and its value at the right, so the
  values of a list (rooms, batteries, departures) stand under each other.
- A long line of words takes two lines where the card has the room, instead of ending in dots.
- Rows and lines of words take a larger face where the card has room for it, never larger than its values.
- A ring: `ring` parts stand as rings, several side by side (the air of a room, the batteries of the house), the value
  large in the middle of its ring and the icon and label under it, all rings of a row as large as the largest
  (Schumey's design, pull request #2). A ring always keeps its icon and label under it, even where the values give
  theirs up for a larger face: its colour says how good a value is, not what it is. On a card with values a ring is compact: it stands among them as tall as their numbers, with its number
  inside (a share beside two counts). On a tile too small for them, their numbers stand as values.
- A badge: an icon field that starts with `#` shows its words in a box of the part's colour, as a line's number in a
  list of departures (`row|4|min|Main station|blue|#16`).
- Values of a shorter row stand under the columns of the row above it instead of spreading over the width.
- Values take the large digits also beside a row with a time or words (`row|15:25||Race day`): only the values that
  stand large count, so two counts over a share and a time are as large as the card lets them be.
- The card keeps its parts in the screen's PSRAM, so the memory Wi-Fi needs stays free.
- Two options of the tile in the inspector (Schumey, pull request #2): **Show the name** (on) and **Values in their
  colour** (off). Both keep a tile as it was by default.
- Needs Tessera 0.4.88 or later.

## 0.5.0 - 2026-10-14
- Large numbers on a large tile: where they fit and every value is a number, the values take the large digits of
  Tessera's climate card. A value with a word in it keeps the face it had.
- Green, yellow, orange, red and blue are Tessera's own colours by meaning (good, moderate, bad, the accent), readable
  on the card in light and dark, as Tessera colours a level.
- Where nothing fits a small tile, its values stand two to a row, or one, instead of being cut short in one row.
- A text beside other parts on a flat tile keeps its words whole where the parts can stand under each other
  instead; labels still come first.
- Needs Tessera 0.4.88 or later: an older one keeps offering 0.4.3.

## 0.4.3 - 2026-10-12
- Up to eight parts on a card instead of six: two full rows of four values. Each tile of the card costs the screen a
  little more memory for it.
- Lines of text and bars across the card get smaller with the values where the tile is short, instead of running out
  at the bottom; where even the smallest size is too large, the card shows the lines that fit whole.

## 0.4.2 - 2026-10-12
- A picture on the Plugins page.

## 0.4.1 - 2026-10-11
- A coloured icon is darker in the light look where it would not read on the card: a yellow one turns ochre on white.

## 0.4.0 - 2026-10-10
- A tap on the tile opens its parts large on a card over the page, with their labels.
- Needs a Tessera from 2026-10-10 or later: an older one shows the card empty under its top bar.

## 0.3.3 - 2026-10-09
- Listed under the topic Home on the Plugins page.
- Needs a Tessera with plugin API 0.7: update the app first.

## 0.3.2 - 2026-10-09
- A label without an icon or a colour always stays, so every number says what it is.
- An icon or a dot in front of a number keeps a little more room from it.

## 0.3.1 - 2026-10-09
- The tile's inspector offers only the sensors that describe a card (with an `elements` attribute).

## 0.3.0 - 2026-10-09
- First release: values, bars and lines of words that a template sensor describes, side by side on a wide tile and
  stacked on any other, in the screen's fonts and colours.

readme.en:
# Rain (DWD)

This use the hacs integration [DWD Precipitation Forecast](https://github.com/stoppegp/ha-dwd-precipitation-forecast)   

When it rains in the next two hours, from a DWD precipitation forecast sensor in Home Assistant: the icon in a circle
that turns blue while it rains or will within the hour, a sentence such as "In 25 min. it rains for 20 min." or "No
rain in the next two hours", the rain now in mm/h, and under it the forecast of the next two hours as bars (light rain
blue, a downpour purple).

## Set up

1. Have a [DWD precipitation forecast sensor](https://github.com/stoppegp/ha-dwd-precipitation-forecast) in Home Assistant whose attributes are `next_start`, `next_end`,
   `next_length` (minutes) and `forecast` (a time and a rain rate in mm/h for every five minutes), such as
   `sensor.dwd_precipitation_forecast_home`. Its state is the rain now.
2. In Tessera, open **Plugins**, **Add with a link**, and paste the link of this repository. Add the plugin to a
   screen; the screen builds.
3. In **Layout**, place the **Rain** tile (2 x 1 or wider) and choose the sensor in its inspector. Only sensors with a
   `forecast` are offered.

## Options

- **Show the chart**: the bars under the words, where the tile has room for them.
- **Forecast step**: the minutes between two values of the forecast, 5 for the DWD nowcast.

## Good to know

- The tile counts down on the screen's own clock; the sensor brings a new forecast every five minutes.
- The chart starts at the first value of the forecast, which the sensor keeps at now.
- It uses no service of its own: everything comes from the sensor in Home Assistant.

readme.en:
# Electricity price

The electricity price now as a tile, with the graph of today and tomorrow on bigger tiles and on a card of its own.
It reads the price sensor of **Nord Pool** (HACS `nordpool`), **ENTSO-e** (`entsoe`), **GE-Spot** (`ge_spot`) or **EPEX Spot** (HACS `epex_spot`, for example `sensor.epex_spot_data_total_price`) in Home Assistant. For GE-Spot, use its price sensor in a currency per kWh (not the cents display).

It runs on every board Tessera supports (`boards: any`), from the CYD to the 10.1-inch screens.

## Set up

1. In Tessera, open **Plugins** and choose **Electricity price**, or choose **Add with a link** and paste
   `https://github.com/Heronimonimo/tessera-electricity-price`. Tick your screens; each builds once.
2. In Layout, place the **Electricity price (Nord Pool)**, **Electricity price (ENTSO-e)**, **Electricity price
   (GE-Spot)** or **Electricity price (EPEX Spot)** tile from the library's Plugins group, at any size from 1x1 up to the whole page. A tile smaller than
   2x2 shows the price with the meter bar; from 2x2 up it adds the graph.
3. In the inspector, choose your price sensor. The list holds only the sensors that fit the tile you placed.
4. Choose the unit, **EUR/kWh** (`0.273`) or **ct/kWh** (`27.3`), and the number of decimals (in ct/kWh at most one).
5. Optionally set your tariff (below).
6. Tap a bar of the graph to see its price and time slot for a few seconds, on a bigger tile and on the full screen card. On a tile, tap that bar again, or beside the bars, to open the card: the price now, the lowest and highest still to come, the day's average, and the graph.

## Your tariff

The sensor gives the market price p. In the inspector you can type what you really pay, and what you get back, as a
formula in p:

| Field | Example | Means |
|---|---|---|
| **Delivery price** | `(p+0.12)*1.21` | Energy tax and surcharge on top, then 21% VAT |
| | `0.25` | A fixed price |
| **Feed-in price** | `p-0.02` | The market price minus your supplier's 2 cents |
| | `0,07` | A fixed feed-in price |

A formula has p, numbers (`0.12` or `0,12`), `+ - * /` and brackets. The numbers are in the sensor's currency per
kWh (0.02, not 2), also when the tile shows cents. An empty delivery price is the sensor's own price; an empty feed-in
price is none. A formula with a typo shows "Check the formula" on the screen in place of the price; the editor
cannot check it for you.

With a feed-in price each bar runs from the feed-in price to the delivery price, so you see the gap between the two
over the day, also when feed-in is the higher one. The tile and the card show the feed-in price of now under the
price. The editor's preview shows the sensor's own price: it cannot work out the formula.

## Bars or a stepped line

In the inspector, **Graph** chooses **Bars** or **Stepped line**. The stepped line follows the price slot by slot in
the same colours as the bars, with a dot for now. With a feed-in price it is a thin grey line under the delivery
price. **Fill under the line** adds a faint fill down to zero, or to the feed-in price. The card shows the graph of
the tile you open it from. **Grid lines** draws solid or dotted lines across the graph at its price labels.

**Next 24 hours only** shows the 24 hours from now instead of today and tomorrow, and takes the meter's range and the
card's average, lowest and highest from those hours. Until tomorrow's prices are in (in the afternoon), they end at
midnight.

## The price in the top bar

Place **Electricity price** on a page's top bar in the editor, under "From plugins". It shows the price now exactly
as your price tile does: the same sensor, formula, unit and decimals. With more than one price tile on the screen, the
first one with a sensor gives it. The top bar needs a price tile on the screen, on any page.

## Good to know

- The graph has a bar for every quarter of an hour when the sensor has quarter prices, else for every hour. A tile
  with more than 100 slots (quarters of today and tomorrow) joins neighbouring quarters into one bar; the card shows
  them all. Past bars are grey, the bar now is the accent colour, and the bars to come are green, amber or red by their
  place between the lowest and highest price. Prices below zero hang under the zero line.
- Tomorrow's bars appear on their own as soon as the sensor has them (the day-ahead prices come in the afternoon).
- The price of now is the current time slot of today's list, as the bar of now shows it, not the sensor's state.
  For ENTSO-e, choose its average-price sensor for a tile: it is the one with the lists (the tile and the top bar
  still show the price of now).
- The unit comes from the sensor (`EUR/kWh` shows as `€/kWh`). A sensor that reports per MWh is shown per kWh.
- On the days the clock changes, the graph has 23 or 25 hours, each where it is on the clock.
- EPEX Spot's total price sensor already holds surcharges and VAT, so its delivery formula can stay empty.
- The EPEX Spot tile and the German translation come from Nekromonger's
  [tessera-strompreis](https://github.com/Nekromonger/tessera-strompreis).

changelog.en:
# Changelog

## 0.12.0
- EPEX Spot: a fourth tile, **Electricity price (EPEX Spot)**, for the sensor of the HACS `epex_spot` integration. Its
  one list of yesterday, today and tomorrow is cut into today and tomorrow by the start of its slots. From
  Nekromonger's [tessera-strompreis](https://github.com/Nekromonger/tessera-strompreis).
- **Next 24 hours only**, on every tile: the graph shows the 24 hours from the slot of now instead of today and
  tomorrow, up to midnight while tomorrow's prices are not in yet. The meter's range and the card's average, lowest
  and highest are of those 24 hours too. The card follows the tile.
- German, from Nekromonger's translation.

## 0.11.0
- The top bar shows the price as your tiles do: the sensor, formula, unit and decimals of a price tile on the screen,
  and the price of the current time slot. The first tile with a sensor gives it. Its own sensor and its two settings
  (Price sensor for the top bar, Top bar: price formula, Top bar: unit) are gone, and so is the permission to read
  that sensor. A screen without a price tile shows no price in the top bar.

## 0.10.0
- The price now in the top bar: place **Electricity price** on a page's top bar in the editor, under "From plugins".
  It reads the price sensor chosen when the plugin is added (Price sensor for the top bar), through a formula of its
  own and in EUR/kWh or ct/kWh: two settings in the plugin's details on the screen's Plugins tab, which change
  without a build. A formula with a typo says "Check the formula".
- The price of now comes from today's list at the current time slot, the same as the bar of now. The ENTSO-e tile
  showed the day's average as the price of now: ENTSO-e keeps its lists only on its average-price sensor, whose
  state is that average (issue #2). Without a list or a set clock, the sensor's state stays the price.

## 0.9.0
- Graph: bars or a stepped line, chosen per tile in the editor. The stepped line follows the price slot by slot in the
  colours of the bars, with a dot for now; a feed-in price is a thin grey line under it. A tapped slot gets a line
  down through it and a dot on each price.
- Fill under the line (on by default): a faint fill down to zero, or to the feed-in price.
- Grid lines (none by default): solid or dotted lines across the graph at the price labels it shows. The lines
  that were there before were a pixel wide by mistake, so none showed.
- The card shows the graph of the tile you open it from.

## 0.8.1
- A tapped bar shows its feed-in price too: after its time on a tile, where it fits, and on the card in the feed-in
  line, with its time slot.

## 0.8.0
- The tariff is a formula you type, one for delivery and one for feed-in: `(p+0.12)*1.21`, `p-0.02`, or a number
  alone for a fixed price. p is the sensor's price per kWh; + - * /, brackets and a decimal point or comma work.
  A formula with a typo shows "Check the formula" in place of the price.
- The a, b and c options of 0.7.0 are gone: type your tariff again as a formula.

## 0.7.0
- Your own tariff on top of the market price: the delivery price is (p + a) × b + c, with a for the energy tax and the
  supplier's surcharge, b for the VAT and c added after it. b 0 and c your price make a fixed price.
- An optional feed-in price, (p + a) × b + c with its own a, b and c. With it each bar of the graph runs from the
  feed-in price up to the delivery price; the colours stay those of the delivery price.
- The feed-in price of now under the price on the meter tile, where it has room, and under the price on the card.

## 0.6.6
- A sensor that reports per MWh shows its price per kWh, in EUR/kWh and in ct/kWh alike. Before, ct/kWh multiplied a
  price per MWh by 100.
- On the days the clock changes (23 or 25 hours), the bar of now, the times under the graph and the time slots of a
  tapped bar and of the highest and lowest price are right. Before, they were an hour off after the change.
- When tomorrow's prices come in another resolution than today's (hours beside quarters), the graph shows them in
  today's, without gaps.
- "Choose a price sensor" and "No price" fit on a small tile and on the card, in every language: without a price
  the message takes the whole row, in a smaller font where needed. Before, it was cut off.

## 0.6.5
- The tiles also take the whole page (`full: true`): a tile as big as the grid, such as 5x5 on a 5x5 grid, was not offered before.
- The editor shows the price with its unit.

## 0.6.4
- The tiles come in every size, from 1x1 up to 9x9 (before, at most 4x3).

## 0.6.3
- Graph: the bars share the whole width of the plot. Before, each bar had a whole number of pixels, so on a screen where 192 quarters did not divide the width the bars took only part of it.

## 0.6.2
- Card: the highest and the lowest price only count from now on, tomorrow included once it is known. A time slot of tomorrow says "Tomorrow" in front.

## 0.6.1
- The card is as wide as the glass, like Tessera's own graph.

## 0.6.0
- Card: the unit behind the average, the highest and the lowest. A tapped bar shows its price under its time slot in the middle, and the price of now stays at the left.

## 0.5.4
- Store picture (store.png) made on the bench.
- Fixes found by the first real build: the GE-Spot tile is registered, no `strlcpy`, the Tomorrow label stays inside the card.
- The name keeps the tile-label font, the price takes what is left.

## 0.5.3
- The graph shows from 2 wide and 2 high; smaller tiles show the price with the meter bar.

## 0.5.2
- Tile with a graph: the name at the left and the price of now at the right, like the small tile. A tapped bar shows its time in place of the name.

## 0.5.1
- Small tile like the meter bar tile: the name at the left, the price with its unit at the right.

## 0.5.0
- GE-Spot as a source: a third tile reads `today_interval_prices` and `tomorrow_interval_prices` (the `value` of each interval).

## 0.4.1
- Tapping a bar works on the full screen card too (needs API 0.12). High, low and average use the font of the history card.

## 0.4.0
- Tap a bar of the graph on a tile to see its price and time slot for a few seconds. Tap it again, or beside the bars, to open the card.

## 0.3.1
- Card header like the history card: price at the left, average in the middle, highest and lowest at the right with their time slot.

## 0.3.0
- Choose the unit: EUR/kWh or ct/kWh.
- Time axis and price axis in the look of Tessera's history graph; the small tile is the meter's bar of cells.

## 0.2.0
- The graph shows quarter-hour prices when the sensor has them.

readme.en:
# Elpris (Energi Data Service)

The Danish electricity price now as a tile, in kr/kWh or øre/kWh, with the graph of today and tomorrow on bigger tiles
and on a card of its own. It reads the price sensor of the **Energi Data Service** integration (HACS
`energidataservice` by MTrab) in Home Assistant, such as one with tariffs and taxes added by the integration.

It runs on every board Tessera supports (`boards: any`), from the CYD to the 10.1-inch screens. It is built on the
[Electricity price](https://github.com/Heronimonimo/tessera-electricity-price) plugin by Heronimonimo.

Tried on a Guition ESP32-4848S040, and on Tessera's bench: the CYD, the Guition, a Waveshare 4.3-inch in portrait
and the 10.1-inch JC8012P4A1.

## Set up

1. Install the Energi Data Service integration in Home Assistant and set up a price sensor for your area (DK1 or DK2).
   For the price you really pay, turn on tariffs, taxes and VAT in the integration.
2. In Tessera, open **Plugins**, choose **Add with a link** and paste this repository's link. Tick your screens; each
   builds once.
3. In Layout, place the **Electricity price (Energi Data Service)** tile from the library's Plugins group, at any size
   from 1x1 up to the whole page. A tile smaller than 2x2 shows the price with the meter bar; from 2x2 up it adds the
   graph.
4. In the inspector, choose your price sensor. The list holds only Energi Data Service sensors.
5. Choose the unit, **kr/kWh** (`2.31`) or **øre/kWh** (`231`), and the number of decimals (in øre at most one).
6. Tap a bar of the graph to see its price and time slot. Tap it again, or beside the bars, to open the card: the
   price now, the lowest and highest still to come, the day's average and the graph.

## Your tariff

The sensor gives the price p in kr/kWh. Leave **Delivery price** empty when the sensor already has tariffs, taxes and
VAT. For a sensor without them you can type a formula in p:

| Field              | Example         | Means                                   |
|--------------------|-----------------|-----------------------------------------|
| **Delivery price** | `(p+0.15)*1.25` | A surcharge on top, then 25% VAT        |
|                    | `2.10`          | A fixed price                           |
| **Feed-in price**  | `p-0.10`        | The price minus your supplier's 10 øre  |

A formula has p, numbers (`0.15` or `0,15`), `+ - * /` and brackets. The numbers are in kr/kWh, also when the tile
shows øre. A formula with a typo shows "Check the formula" on the screen in place of the price.

## Good to know

- The graph has a bar for every quarter of an hour when the sensor has quarter prices, else for every hour. Past bars
  are grey, the bar now is the accent colour, and the bars to come are green, amber or red by their place between the
  lowest and highest price.
- Tomorrow's bars appear as soon as the sensor has them (Energi Data Service gets them in the early afternoon).
- The price of now is the slot of now in today's list, not the sensor's state.
- **Cheapest hours** marks the cheapest hours to come (up to 6) with a dark stroke over their bars: each on its own,
  or as the cheapest stretch in a row (**Cheapest hours as**), handy for a dishwasher or a car. The card names them in
  its day row. Only known prices count, not the forecast.
- **Period** can show the next 24 or 48 hours from now in place of whole days. The known prices end at midnight
  tomorrow (tomorrow's come in the early afternoon); after them the graph shows Carnot's forecast in fainter bars, when
  the forecast is on in Energi Data Service (its options, with a free Carnot account). The card's low and high come
  from the known prices only.
- On the days the clock changes, the graph has 23 or 25 hours, each where it is on the clock.
- **Electricity price** can also stand in a page's top bar (editor, "From plugins"): the price now of your first price
  tile.

# Changelog

## 0.6.0

  a dark stroke over their bars, each on its own or as the cheapest stretch in a row. The card names them in its day
  row ("Cheapest 02:00–05:00"). Only known prices count, not the forecast. Off (0) until you set it.

## 0.5.0

- **Next 24 hours** and **Next 48 hours** now fill the hours after the known prices with Carnot's forecast from
  Energi Data Service, in fainter bars, so the graph always reaches 24 or 48 hours ahead. Turn on the forecast
  (Carnot) in the integration's options to get it; without it the graph ends where the prices end, as before.
- The card's low and high still come from the known prices only.

## 0.4.0

- **Period** can now show only the hours to come: the next 24 or the next 48 hours from the hour of now, without the
  hours that have passed. The next 48 go as far as the prices do (midnight tomorrow). On the card, the low and high
  are those of the hours the graph shows.

## 0.3.0

- New option **Period**: today and tomorrow (48 hours, as before) or today only (24 hours). Nothing to do: tiles
  keep showing both days until you change it.

## 0.2.0

- New option **Price per**: every quarter of an hour, or each hour as the average of its quarters. The price now,

- First version: the electricity price now from an Energi Data Service sensor, in kr/kWh or øre/kWh, with a graph of

- Built on the Electricity price plugin by Heronimonimo (MIT).

readme.en:
# Energy flow

Electricity at home with solar panels on one tile, in the spirit of Home Assistant's energy dashboard.

**The tile** shows the sun, the house and the grid side by side: what the panels make now, what the house uses, and
what comes from the grid or goes back to it. Arrows show where the power flows; a circle takes its colour while power
flows there (amber for the sun, blue for power from the grid, green for power to it). Under them, when there is room:

- a bar of the house's use, amber as far as the sun covers it, blue for the rest ("Solar covers 46 %");
- the day so far ("Today: solar 3.4 kWh · from the grid 5.2 kWh");
- what the panels made against today's forecast, as a bar.

It fits any size from 1 x 1 to 6 x 3: on a narrow tile it shows the grid and, under it, the sun. Each part shows
only while there is room for it and a sensor for it. **A tap** opens a card: at the left the flow as in Home Assistant's energy card, the sun above, the grid and the
house below, joined by lines that take their colour and a dot where power flows; at the right every chosen sensor in
a row of its own (grid, solar, house, coverage, solar today, forecast with how much of it is made, grid today).

## Set up

1. In Tessera, open **Plugins**, **Add with a link**, and paste the link of this repository. Add the plugin to a
   screen.
2. In the plugin's details on the screen's Plugins tab, under **When building**, choose the sensors:
   - **Grid power** (needed): your meter's power in W or kW, positive while power comes from the grid and negative
     while it goes back. A meter that counts the other way round: switch on **Invert the grid** on the tile.
   - **Solar power**: what the panels make now.
   - **Solar today**, **Grid today**: today's energy in kWh, for the day so far.
   - **Solar coverage**: a sensor in % if you have one; without it the share is worked out from solar and grid.
   - **Forecast today**: today's solar forecast in kWh (Forecast.Solar, Solcast).
   Leave out what you do not have. **Save and build**.
3. In **Layout**, place the **Energy** tile.

## Good to know

- The house's use is grid + solar. A battery is not part of it yet.
- W and kW, Wh and kWh are both understood: the plugin reads each sensor's unit.

readme.it:
# Film stasera

Un tile con i film in TV stasera in Italia: l'orario d'inizio, il titolo e, sotto, il canale e il genere. Appartiene
a **un sensore di Home Assistant** e non scarica niente da internet.

## Come si usa

1. In Home Assistant crea il sensore `sensor.film_stasera`: lo stato e' il numero di film, con quattro attributi
   della stessa lunghezza, una voce per film: `titles`, `channels`, `starts` (secondi dal 1970) e `genres`. Facoltativi: `groups` (un numero da 1 a 4 per film, il colore del pallino
   davanti al nome del canale: 1 blu, 2 ambra, 3 verde, 4 viola; 0 o assente: nessun pallino) e `stale` (true o
   false: la guida e' vecchia).
2. Aggiungi il plugin a uno schermo in Tessera. Lo schermo si ricompila una volta.
3. In Layout metti il tile **Film stasera** dalla libreria (gruppo Plugin), da 1x1 a 4x4: mostra tutti i film che
   ci stanno. Poi scegli il sensore nell'ispettore.

## Da sapere

- Su un tile largo (circa 13 cm o piu', come quattro colonne di uno schermo da 7 pollici) i film vanno su due colonne,
  uno dopo l'altro, cosi' una serata intera sta in una pagina.
- Un film iniziato meno di due ore e mezza fa resta nel tile, con l'orario nel colore d'accento: la guida non ha gli
  orari di fine. Il tile segue l'orologio dello schermo, quindi un film esce dalla lista da solo.
- Quando non resta nessun film lo dice, e quando la guida e' vecchia lo scrive accanto alla data.
- Non servono chiavi ne' account.
- Provato su un vero Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-7B (7 pollici, firmware Tessera 0.55.0). Nel banco di prova dei
  plugin (`tools/preview.py`) si disegna senza avvisi anche sul Waveshare da 5 pollici e sul CYD (2,8 pollici).

## Modalità e pulsante Aggiorna

Il tile ha due modalità. **Film** (quella di partenza) elenca i film di stasera. **Programmi** elenca, per ogni canale in
ordine di numero del telecomando, il programma di prima serata e quello di seconda serata, ognuno con il suo orario;
quando i canali non entrano, la pagina cambia da sola ogni 8 secondi. Un tocco sul tile cambia modalità; l'opzione
"Modalità iniziale" dice da quale parte.

Quando mancano i dati (il sensore non ha un valore, o la sua guida non è di oggi) il tile lo dice e mostra un pulsante
**Aggiorna**. Un tocco chiede a Home Assistant di aggiornare il sensore, cioè di lanciare lo script che scarica la guida.
Lo schermo deve poter eseguire azioni di Home Assistant.

Per i Programmi il sensore ha bisogno degli attributi `prog_channels`, `prog_groups`, `prog1_titles`, `prog1_starts`,
`prog2_titles` e `prog2_starts`: arrivano con la versione 0.3 dello script `film-stasera-ha`. L'app manda a ogni tile al
massimo 2600 byte: in una serata con molti film le liste vengono tagliate alla stessa lunghezza.

# Films tonight

A tile with the films on Italian TV tonight: the start time, the title, and under it the channel and the genre. It
belongs to **one sensor of Home Assistant** and fetches nothing from the internet itself.

## Set up

1. In Home Assistant, make the sensor `sensor.film_stasera` (the one this plugin was written for): a sensor whose
   state is the number of films, with four attributes of the same length, one entry per film: `titles`, `channels`,
   `starts` (seconds since 1970) and `genres`. Optional: `groups` (a number 1 to 4 per film, the colour of the dot before
   the channel's name: 1 blue, 2 amber, 3 green, 4 purple; 0 or missing draws no dot) and `stale` (true or false: the
   guide is old).
2. Add the plugin to a screen in Tessera. The screen builds once.
3. In Layout, place the **Films tonight** tile from the library's Plugins group (1x1 up to 4x4: it shows as many films
   as fit) and choose the sensor in the inspector.

## Good to know

- On a wide tile (about 13 cm or more, such as four columns of a 7-inch screen) the films run in two columns, one after
  the other, so a whole evening fits on one page.
- A film that started less than two and a half hours ago stays on the tile, with its time in the accent colour: the
  guide has no end times. The tile follows the screen's own clock, so a film leaves the list on its own.
- When no film is left it says so. When the guide is old it says that beside the date.
- It needs no key and no account.
- Tried on a real Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-7B (7 inch, Tessera firmware 0.55.0). On the plugin bench
  (`tools/preview.py`) it also draws without warnings on the 5-inch Waveshare and on the CYD (2.8 inch).

## Modes and the Update button

The tile has two modes. **Films** (the default) lists tonight's films. **Programmes** lists, for each channel in the
order of the remote, the prime-time programme and the late one, each with its time; when the channels do not fit, the
page turns by itself every 8 seconds. A tap on the tile changes the mode; the tile option "Start mode" says which one it
starts in.

When there is no data (the sensor has no value, or its guide is not today's) the tile says so and shows an **Update**
button. A tap asks Home Assistant to update the sensor, which runs the script that fetches the guide. The screen must be
allowed to perform Home Assistant actions.

The sensor needs the attributes `prog_channels`, `prog_groups`, `prog1_titles`, `prog1_starts`, `prog2_titles` and
`prog2_starts` for the Programmes mode: they come with the 0.3 version of the script `film-stasera-ha`. The app sends a
tile at most 2600 bytes: on an evening with many films the lists are cut to the same length.

  mode works as before and the Programmes mode says there are no programmes.
- The tile asks for a little more room in the screen's layout memory (11000 bytes).
- A long press counts as a tap. On some screens the finger's release reaches the app late, so a quick tap was read as a
  long press, which a plugin never hears, and the tile sometimes ignored it. The tile also repaints only when
  something changed (page, minute, data), not every second.
